questions.stem: The Chief Justice of India is appointed by the:
questions.explanation: Art 124(2) — the Chief Justice of India and other Supreme Court judges are appointed by the President. Since the Second Judges Case (1993) the Collegium (CJI + senior SC judges) recommends names; the government's role is limited. The Second and Third Judges Cases gave the Collegium its present form. The NJAC Act was struck down by the SC in 2015 as unconstitutional.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The retirement age of a Supreme Court judge is:
questions.explanation: Art 124(2) — SC judges retire at 65; HC judges at 62 (raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment in 1963). Tribunals and various commissions often have different age ceilings (often 65 or 70). A judge can be removed before that only by impeachment (proved misbehaviour or incapacity, 2/3 special majority in both Houses).

questions.stem: The 'Basic Structure' doctrine of the Indian Constitution was propounded by the Supreme Court in:
questions.explanation: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — a 13-judge bench (largest ever at the time) held by 7-6 that Parliament's power under Art 368 does not extend to altering the Basic Structure of the Constitution. Golaknath (1967) had earlier held that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights, but was overruled. Minerva Mills (1980) strengthened the Basic Structure doctrine further. Shankari Prasad (1951) had held the opposite — that amendments could abridge FRs.

questions.stem: The Supreme Court of India consists of the Chief Justice and not more than:
questions.explanation: Currently — CJI + up to 33 other judges (total strength 34), as per the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019. Earlier strengths — originally CJI + 7 (1950), raised in stages. The SC sits in New Delhi; the CJI may, with the President's approval, set up a bench elsewhere, though this has rarely happened.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 32 — invoked to file a writ directly in the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights — was called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by:
questions.explanation: Ambedkar, chairing the Drafting Committee, described Art 32 as the 'very soul' / 'heart and soul' of the Constitution during the Constituent Assembly debates. Art 32 itself is a Fundamental Right — the right to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of other FRs. It cannot be suspended except during a National Emergency (as restricted by 44th Amendment).

questions.stem: Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to:

options.option_text: Extend its jurisdiction to new areas

questions.explanation: Art 137 — the Supreme Court has the power to review any judgment pronounced by it; this is the 'review jurisdiction'. The beyond-review 'curative petition' (developed by the SC in Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002) is a narrow final remedy even after a review is dismissed. Art 139A — transfer of cases between HCs; Art 141 — SC's declarations of law bind all other courts.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The first Chief Justice of independent India was:
questions.explanation: Harilal J. Kania served as the first Chief Justice of India from 26 January 1950 till his sudden death in November 1951. He was succeeded by M. Patanjali Sastri. Mehr Chand Mahajan (not 'M.C. Mahajan' — same person) was CJI from 1954 and is also known for leading Kashmir's accession negotiations. The Supreme Court of India itself was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.
